waypoints.name: South Climb / Cold Springs Trailhead
waypoints.directions: From Trout Lake, drive north on Mt Adams Road to the FR 23 junction and bear right about a mile to the signed FR 80 turn for South Climb. Follow FR 80 for 3.7 miles to FR 8040, then FR 8040 for 8.1 miles to its end at the South Climb / Cold Springs trailhead; it is steep and narrow with sharp switchbacks, so no RVs or trailers. Self-issue a free wilderness permit at the trailhead, and buy the Mt. Adams Climbing Pass online beforehand to go above 7,000 ft.

waypoints.name: Mount Adams Summit
waypoints.directions: Follow South Climb Trail #183 up an old roadbed through the burn, across the Round the Mountain Trail and the PCT, and up Crescent Ridge beside the Crescent Glacier to the Lunch Counter, a rocky bench at about 9,250-9,400 ft. Climb the south-facing snowfield of the South Spur about 2,400 ft to Piker's Peak, the false summit, then drop to the saddle and climb the last 600 ft or so of the summit cone to the old lookout on top.

waypoints.name: Climbers Bivouac Trailhead
waypoints.note: Highest vehicle access on the south side via FR-90/FR-83/FR-81/Spur 830; Ptarmigan Trail #216A starts here, and a climbing permit is required above 4,800 ft.
waypoints.directions: From Cougar, follow FR-90, FR-83, FR-81 and Spur 830 to the Climbers Bivouac trailhead at 3,700 ft, the highest vehicle access on this side of the mountain. Ptarmigan Trail #216A starts from the parking area. A climbing permit is required year-round above 4,800 ft and is checked at or near the trailhead; permits sell on Recreation.gov and release on the 1st of the prior month. Climbers Bivouac and the summer route are typically open and snow-free from late June through October.

waypoints.name: Ptarmigan Trail / Loowit Trail junction
waypoints.note: Ptarmigan Trail #216A meets the Loowit Trail (#216) here after climbing 900 ft through second-growth forest; continue straight/south to keep ascending toward timberline.
waypoints.directions: From the parking area pick up the signed Ptarmigan Trail #216A and follow it through second-growth forest for a little over two miles, gaining roughly 1,000 ft at an easy grade to the point where the Loowit Trail cuts across. Keep going straight and uphill rather than turning onto the Loowit. This stretch holds the only shade and the only seasonal creeklets on the route, and nothing above is dependable, so most parties carry all their water from the car.

waypoints.name: Timberline / permit-zone boundary
waypoints.note: Trees give out and the route opens onto Monitor Ridge's lava flows; this is the start of the year-round permit zone above which every climber must carry a self-issued or reserved permit.
waypoints.directions: A few hundred yards further the trees thin out and the tread gives way to the open lava and pumice of the ridge itself. This is the 4,800 ft line above which every climber must be carrying a permit, so it is the last place to sort that out. Before committing to the slope, find the first of the wooden posts and confirm the line you will be following.

waypoints.name: End of wooden route-marker posts
waypoints.note: Large wooden posts mark the boulder-hop route up Monitor Ridge to about this elevation; above here the tread disappears and the line is unmarked loose rock, pumice, and ash.
waypoints.directions: Above timberline the route follows a widely spaced line of tall wooden posts up boulder ribs and blocky old lava for about 2,200 ft; the rock ribs travel far better than the ash gullies beside them. Losing the post line in fog or low cloud is the biggest route-finding problem on the climb and a small drift off it puts you on steep, loose, off-route ground, so sight the next post before leaving the last. The posts run out near a GPS monitoring station at about 7,000 ft.

waypoints.name: Mount St. Helens summit (crater rim high point)
waypoints.note: True summit is about a quarter mile west along the crescent crater rim from where Monitor Ridge tops out; on clear days it offers views into the 1980-eruption horseshoe crater and lava dome.
waypoints.directions: The high point is a short walk west along the crescent of the rim from where Monitor Ridge tops out. Stay on the outer side of the crest the whole way and keep the same distance off the lip; there is nothing gained by walking the edge for the view into the crater.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek Trailhead (Cascade River Road)
waypoints.directions: Drive Cascade River Road east from Marblemount for about 20 miles to the Eldorado trailhead pullout, about 3 miles short of the road's end at Cascade Pass, roughly 2,100 feet; the first ten miles are paved and the rest is gravel and washboard. There's a pit toilet at the parking area. The road typically doesn't open until late May or June, depending on snowpack. Camping here needs a North Cascades National Park backcountry permit reserved in advance, but the permit itself must be picked up in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center before you drive up.

waypoints.name: Eldorado / Inspiration Glacier camp
waypoints.directions: Walk about 90 ft back down the road and cross the Cascade River on the log, then go about 100 ft straight away from the river to the climbers' path. It climbs steeply through timber for about 1,500 ft to a boulder field; follow cairns up it, staying climber's right of Eldorado Creek, into Eldorado Creek Basin. Cross the ridge at about 6,100 ft into Roush Basin, take talus and slabs onto the Eldorado Glacier, rope up, and climb it to camp near 7,500 ft.

waypoints.name: Inspiration Glacier
waypoints.directions: Roped, cross the nearly flat Inspiration Glacier toward the obvious low gap near the east end of Eldorado's East Ridge. Take a bearing from camp, because the glacier is featureless in cloud. Pass north through the gap onto the glacier slopes north of the ridge.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Peak summit
waypoints.directions: Climb west up the glacier slopes north of the ridge, keeping the crest on your left and probing suspect snow bridges, to where the slope steepens below the knife-edge. Follow the narrow, often corniced snow crest to the small summit. An axe and crampons are essential, and many parties place pickets along the crest.
